content:
{'translation': 'The Labour Union (勞聯) today (27th) released a survey on the working conditions of cleaning workers, revealing that the majority of outsourced cleaning workers have not been provided with adequate equipment during hot weather. For instance, 40% have not been provided with drinking water or towels to cool down, and even those who did receive such supplies found the quality to be inconsistent—such as being given unclean drinking water or rubber gloves that trap heat. The Labour Union also noted that some outsourced workers under the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department (FEHD) reported that when they brought their own cooling gear such as ice sleeves and portable fans, and were inspected by the FEHD Service Quality Inspection Group, supervisors had to write reports explaining the reasons. Some supervisors had told workers that "the higher-ups disapprove" and instructed them to stop. The Labour Union suggested that the FEHD incorporate cooling equipment into the standard uniform for cleaning workers. In response to enquiries, the FEHD refuted these claims, stating that the Labour Union\'s remarks regarding the equipment provided to outsourced cleaning workers were "inaccurate and inconsistent with the facts."'}

{'translation': 'The Labour Union and related unions and organisations interviewed cleaning workers and received 546 responses, of which 82% of respondents expressed a desire to improve heat-related work arrangements.'}

{'translation': 'The survey was conducted by the Labour Union, the Concern Group on Occupational Safety and Health, and the Hong Kong Environmental Services Employees Union Federation between May and July this year, covering cleaning workers under the FEHD, outsourced by the FEHD, and private-sector cleaning workers. A total of 546 valid responses were received.'}

{'translation': 'Labour Union Legislative Council member Lam Chun-sing (林振昇) noted that the survey showed only about 60% of workers said their company provided drinking water or towels for cooling, meaning 40% of employers did not provide such basic equipment. Even when supplies were provided, the quality varied—some workers received unclean drinking water or rubber gloves that trap heat—and the quantity of supplies received also differed among workers at the same company. The provision of other cooling equipment was even worse: 80% were not provided with ice sleeves, 63% had no portable fans, and 53% had no wide-brimmed hats.'}

{'translation': 'The Labour Union said it had received reports from outsourced workers that after bringing their own cooling gear, they were inspected by FEHD personnel, requiring supervisors to write reports explaining the situation, and had been told to stop after supervisors said "the higher-ups disapprove."'}

{'translation': 'Labour Union Director of External Affairs Li Zhuoshen (李卓燊) added that workers who brought their own ice sleeves and fans had reported that when inspected by the FEHD "Service Quality Inspection Group," supervisors had to write reports explaining why workers carried such equipment. Some supervisors had also told workers that "the higher-ups disapprove" and ordered them to stop bringing their own cooling supplies. Such situations were not confined to individual districts. He suggested that the FEHD incorporate cooling equipment into the standard uniform for cleaning workers, either provided uniformly by the department or supplied by the workers themselves.'}

{'translation': 'Li Zhuoshen suggested that the FEHD incorporate cooling equipment into the standard uniform for cleaning workers, either provided uniformly by the department or supplied by the workers themselves.'}

{'translation': '7% of workers had suffered heatstroke; over 80% continued to work as usual'}

{'translation': 'Another set of survey data indicated that 7% of respondents had experienced heatstroke, but over 85% of them did not take leave as a result. Hong Kong Environmental Services Employees Union Federation Chairperson Ng Kam-lin (吳金蓮) noted that workers on duty generally do not receive notifications when the Very Hot Weather Warning is in effect, and work locations vary daily—they "can only figure things out on their own." In most cases, they could only seek shade for brief rests, and many more simply endured the heat and only rested after completing their work. Ng also mentioned that FEHD staff conduct inspections from time to time, and if workers are photographed resting or accused of shirking, the company would be fined and then penalise the workers, causing anxiety among workers.'}

{'translation': 'Among respondents, 7% of cleaning workers had experienced heatstroke, but over 85% of them did not take leave as a result. Additionally, 74% of workers were unable to rest in well-ventilated spaces.'}

{'translation': 'Lam Chun-sing pointed out that cleaning workers are mostly elderly and particularly value their job opportunities, so they may not take leave easily even after suffering heatstroke. He suggested incorporating age as a factor in determining heat-related rest periods. He also noted that the current rest environment for workers is poor—74% of respondents were unable to rest in well-ventilated spaces, with main rest locations being outdoors, refuse collection points, stairwells, or even toilets, and 10% had no time or space to rest at all. Regarding the current "Guidance Notes on Prevention of Heat Stroke at Work," which states that if cooling or ventilation equipment is provided at the workplace, rest periods can be correspondingly reduced, Lam said this makes it difficult for workers to rest based on actual temperatures, and the authorities should review the arrangements.'}

{'translation': 'Labour Union Secretary-General and Legislative Council member Chau Siu-chung (周小松) noted that the current 10 heat监测 stations across the territory do not reflect the conditions of all workplaces—even at the same temperature of 37 degrees, different humidity levels have different impacts on workers. He proposed that the government could subsidise the installation of Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) meters at some high-temperature work locations, such as outdoor areas of the airport and Chinese restaurant kitchens, so employers could reference the data to arrange rest periods for employees. He also called for continued establishment of rest stations.'}

{'translation': 'The Labour Union recommended that the government revise the provisions on rest period reductions in the guidance notes and suggested that authorities subsidise the installation of Wet Bulb Globe Temperature meters at high-temperature work locations.'}

{'translation': 'The Labour Union survey also showed that 54% of cleaning workers earn a monthly salary between HK$13,000 and HK$16,000, while nearly 25% of cleaning workers earn less than HK$13,000 per month. The Labour Union noted that these cleaning workers are mostly employed by private companies.'}

{'translation': "FEHD: Labour Union's claims inconsistent with facts; contractors required to provide heat prevention supplies under contracts"}

{'translation': 'In response to enquiries, the FEHD refuted the claims, stating that the Labour Union\'s remarks regarding equipment for outsourced cleaning workers were "inconsistent with the facts," and that the department has established a clear and specific system for occupational safety and health. The department stated that under current service contracts, contractors must provide work uniforms and personal protective equipment that meet specifications, including uniforms with sweat-wicking, breathable, and reflective functions, sun hats, and heat prevention supplies such as ice sleeves as needed.'}

{'translation': 'The department also stated that since 2022, contracts have explicitly required contractors to provide portable waist-mounted fans for outdoor workers; the heat prevention requirements of the Labour Department\'s "Guidance Notes on Prevention of Heat Stroke at Work" have been incorporated into contracts, requiring contractors to conduct heat risk assessments and formulate corresponding work and rest arrangements, and to clearly communicate these to employees. The department also ensures that drinking water, rest spaces, cleaning water, and toilet facilities are available across various work locations.'}

{'translation': 'The FEHD also stated that it is proceeding with renovation of off-street refuse collection points as planned, providing changing, storage, rest, and meal facilities for staff as well as basic electrical appliances where feasible. Approximately 190 solar-powered cooling rest stations have been set up. At the enforcement level, the department said a demerit points system has been established to monitor and ensure contractors implement measures through regular inspections. For violations, serious default notices may be issued, along with service fee deductions and demerit points. If accumulations reach the upper limit within a specified period, contractors will be suspended from bidding on relevant government service contracts.'}
